sourceInformation.genre: Arcade co-op dungeon crawler (top-down hack-and-shoot with maze exploration)
sourceInformation.perspective: Three-quarter overhead (the engine's threequarter view); top-down and isometric selectable in Settings or with V
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.2 (the dist/handoff engine, patched: 9 small changes in ENGINE-CHANGES.md), HTML5 Canvas 2D, Web Audio, optional WebGPU lighting, AI Hub session client 1.4.0 (Session Protocol v1); no other libraries; tests on Node 24 (node:vm, headless) and Playwright 1.63.0 (headless Chromium)
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's PS1-era 2D look at res ps1: procedural HD Humanoid and Blob rigs, textured TileMap walls and floors, canvas lighting with torches and glows, particles. Three realms (the Larder: plank floors and grey stone; the Ossuary: bone walls on dark slate; the Furnace Gut: brick over glowing lava, falling ash) and the Banquet hall. New art: four dressed heroes with a new axe, bow, shield and horned helmet; the Shade ghost rig; seven generators and the floor pieces as E.SHAPES data with damage states; sprites for keys, treasure, potions, amulets and projectiles; the tumbling Iron Gauntlet. Generic props (ham, loaf, platter, soup, kegs, candles, coffins, banners) are CC0 entries cut from the engine's asset store (Kenney, KayKit).
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's procedural system: rigs posed every step from velocity and state, E.MOVES attacks through E.Attack and E.Combo (a melee set per class), poses (cast, cheer, die, guard), hurt and expression states. New: the Ranger's bow draw, throws per class, the starving hunch, the eating squash, rank loss as a shrink, the Shade's fluttering hem and gaping mouth, monster wind-ups (raised club, glowing imp mouth, landing shadows, the fryars fading in smoke), generators that breathe and crumble, heroes sinking down the stairs, rising again, and King Famish's plates, stomp, feast, charge and fall.
sourceInformation.audio: All synthesized in code with no audio files: nine original chip songs in the engine's step notation (title march, one per realm, the hoard jig, the King with a layer per phase, the ending fanfare, the game-over dirge, the initials loop) with dynamic horde-drum and heartbeat layers; about 60 synthesized sound effects; Babble, a formant gibberish voice synth (Animalese style) for the Gaunt narrator, the four heroes, the King and the monsters, on its own Voices volume.
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1 in shared-world mode, 1-4 players: the host's copy runs the world (or a server copy with no player), clients move their own hero at once and show the rest from 10-per-second snapshots and reliable event batches; the game's own card, time-up standings with stats and awards. Outside a session: solo and local couch co-op for 1-4 on one screen (keyboard halves and gamepads, drop-in and drop-out).
sourceInformation.testing: One command (node tests/run.mjs) runs six suites and prints only failures and a count: 383 checks, 0 failed. floors (every floor solvable with its own keys and matching its brief), sim (117 checks, system by system, and each engine change), play (the whole game played by two bots from the title to Descent II, twice, with the same state hash; a no-cheat balance smoke; the 90 s attract loop; four local players), net (a fake hub running 3 game copies with 150 ms latency, jitter and 5% loss, and a server round), ui (the built single file in headless Chromium from file://, attract timer, mouse on the class cards, a touch-only device), hub (the real AI Hub harness in all four configurations). Screenshots at 1280x720 and 1920x1080 for the look.
sourceInformation.research: No web research. Read the engine handoff (README, API.md, the relevant AI_GUIDE.md sections, the adventure kit, the asset card) and the AI Hub protocol (README, session.js, the harness and the arena example). Gauntlet facts from the model's own knowledge.
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown
sourceInformation.usage: Cost and tokens unknown (no usage meter is visible inside the session). Session time about 1 hour 15 minutes of wall clock (05:02 to about 06:17 on 2026-11-04).

testingFeedback: About 26 real issues. Scripts caught 15: the floor validator found 5 broken floors (stairs walled off by lava, a door corridor one row off its room, unreachable platters, two items overwritten by later placements), the bot playthroughs found 4 (gnasher waves ignoring the monster cap, the bot unable to see the King over the low banquet table, and a co-op deadlock where the shared-screen leash froze a party split by a transporter, on two floors), the sim suite found 1 (a run could reach the high-score table after a cheat was turned off again), and loading found 5 (undefined floors, two constants read before their declaration, a seeded-random harness error, a stale build read by a tool). Screenshots and a browser probe found 11 look and layout problems (the camera zoom never applied because a scene method named camera() replaced the camera option, no camera bounds, walls and floors the same colour, captions over the boss bar, names over scores, overflowing class cards, missing font glyphs, an oversized score table, flat glow discs, a dimmed initials header, a cramped session card). About 20 more failures were mistakes in the tests themselves.

Six were critical: two unsolvable floors, the transporter and leash deadlock (a couch co-op party could be stuck on floor 4 for good), the banquet stall that kept the King alive, and two load-order errors that would have stopped the game from starting.

The bots playing every floor, first one floor at a time and then the whole descent: they found the deadlock and the boss stall that no single-system check would have shown, and the full run doubled as the determinism test.

The first version of the sim suite's direct-intent checks: 19 failures, 18 of them the tests' own set-up (heroes with a player's input had their intent rewritten each step, the arrival throw cooldown, cells that were walls), so it cost more than it found at first.
engineFeedback: Everything is drawn by code with real 3D rigs, so a dozen dressed characters, new weapons and set pieces took a few lines each; and the exact fixed step with game.advance made headless playthroughs of the whole game, and three networked copies in lockstep, run in seconds.

Yes, a few times. A scene method I named camera() silently replaced the scene's camera option, so the zoom never applied; the three-quarter view's scale of 1.5 meant zoom 1 showed only about 18 tiles; I guessed groundArc's argument order wrong once; and E.Menu draws at scale 1, too small for a TV, so I wrote a larger menu.

The split between the simulation, intents and the view, which made one hero controller serve local players, the bot (attract mode and tests) and the network; then the shared-world netcode on top of it (snapshots with an area of interest, event batches, puppets eased between snapshots, a send budget).

The size of the API: the right helper usually exists, but finding it and its exact signature in a 190 KB index takes time, and a wrong guess often fails silently (a draw that does nothing) rather than with a warning.

Nine small patches (ENGINE-CHANGES.md): E1 a flow field to several targets, E2 new weapons, a shield and a horned helmet, E3 bouncing bullets and the wall cell in onWall, E4 Options ignored while Create is held (the hub's rule), E5 PlayStation button symbols by default for every player, E6 a TV scale and setting-row screens for the HTML menus, E7 initials typed by any player with extra fields kept, E8 a voice audio bus and Voices volume, E9 the keyboard's left half keeps the mouse.
A built-in 10-foot mode: the HTML menus scaled for a TV and a canvas menu widget at a larger text size with mouse hover, since every console-style game needs both and each one rebuilds them.
promptFeedback: The concrete, checkable deliverables (the file names, the exit-interview shape, the feedback sections) together with real freedom over the design, and a plan that had already made the decisions, so the work went to building rather than debating.

The plan carries another run's model and timestamp in its file names (it says to use TASK.md's, which I did); the title rule asks for 50 brainstormed titles and a random pick while the plan has already picked one; and Usage asks for cost and tokens that are not visible from inside the session.

Fitting everything into one tested, polished build: nine floors, two treasure rooms and a boss, four classes, shared-world netcode that passes the real harness, couch co-op, a 10-foot interface for pad, keyboard and mouse, the attract mode and the dev tools.

Say whether the plan's title is kept or re-rolled; give a time or token budget; hand the agent its usage numbers (or drop the field); and say where large dev-only files such as node_modules should live in a shared run folder.

aiHub.name: Gauntletdown
aiHub.description: A one-to-four player co-op dungeon crawl inspired by Gauntlet: blast through hordes, smash monster generators and eat before your life force runs out. Play together on one screen, or online in AI Hub sessions.
aiHub.controls: Move WASD/left stick · Aim mouse/right stick · Fire click or Space/R2 · Magic right-click or Q/△ · Plant Shift/L2 · Pause Esc/Options
